newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao resigns as Congress bloc's chief.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao resigns as Congress bloc's chief.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Thursday stepped down as chief of the Congress party's parliamentary delegation, his last party post, amid a flurry of corruption charges, his aides said.
"I submit my resignation from the leadership of the Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP)," Rao's single-line resignation letter said.

Rao, who spearheaded India's move away from socialist economic controls to open markets, led the country from 1991 until last May when the 111-year-old Congress suffered its worst defeat in general elections.

Rao had been served an ultimatum to quit by Congress president Sitaram Kesri after parliamentary deputies passed an unprecedented resolution on Wednesday asking him to resign in the interests of the party's unity.
Rao has also requested the party leadership to call a meeting of the CPP so that he may thank its 229 members, lawmakers in both houses of parliament.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's shaky ruling United Front coalition depends on Congress for crucial support.
The 75-year-old politician has been charged in three separate corruption cases. He denies any wrongdoing in the cases which are before trial judges.
The spate of allegations forced him to step down as Congress president in September and has undercut his authority.

The campaign to drive Rao from the last pedestal of power was part of a broader effort to revive Congress's flagging fortunes, intimately tied to Rao's wily manoeuvring during his last years in power and, more recently, his legal woes.
Analysts fear Rao's departure could lead to a tussle among Congress heavyweights for control of the party's parliamentary bloc, giving the United Front some breathing space.
"Rao has resigned and it is up to the Congress president to take whatever decision he wants," party official Ved Prakash told Reuters.
"When the Congress Working committee is not meeting, the Congress president has all the powers and he can take a decision," Prakash said.
The prospect of a rejuvenated Congress has sent tremors through Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition.
The government needs the support of Congress, with control over 142 deputies in the 545-member lower house, to survive.
Preoccupied with its own internal problems, Congress has to date been a mild critic of Deve Gowda's minority government.
